content:
Epic Games has filed a response to Apple's request for the court to order settlement talks in the long-running App Store lawsuit. Here are the details.

Epic argues there is no benefit to court-ordered settlement talks

Last Thursday, Apple filed its proposed fee structure for completing in-app purchases via systems other than the App Store in the United States.

Under Apple's proposed structure, the company would charge a commission of up to 15% on transactions completed through alternative payment systems.

The same day, Apple filed another motion asking Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to order both parties to attend a settlement conference.

In its motion, Apple said that "discussing potential settlement proposals in a confidential, non-adversarial setting would increase the chance of reaching a pragmatic resolution, thereby avoiding prolonged remand proceedings."

Epic has now responded to Apple's motion, stating that while the company "has been and remains willing to consider any serious settlement proposal Apple may offer, provided it introduces competition and benefits all developers," it "does not believe that referring the parties to a settlement conference at this stage would meaningfully advance the prospects of such a settlement."

Epic added in its response that "if the Court orders referral to a settlement conference, Epic will participate in good faith."

It is now up to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to decide whether to refer the case to a settlement conference. Apple has requested that the conference be conducted under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.

9to5Mac's Take

Apple has repeatedly attempted to narrow the scope of Judge Gonzalez Rogers's injunction concerning transactions outside the App Store. Apple has particularly argued that, because Epic's lawsuit is not a class action, the injunction should not apply broadly to other developers.

For example, in one of its appeals, Apple argued that developers seeking similar relief could file their own lawsuits rather than benefit from Epic's injunction. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected Apple's attempt to narrow the injunction on this basis, ruling that limiting it to Epic and its affiliates would not provide Epic with the full relief it sought.

This rationale is also consistent with Epic's publicly stated position throughout most of the case — that its fight is not limited to its own business interests but aims to benefit developers more broadly.

In its motion requesting referral to confidential settlement talks, Apple did not indicate what proposals it might put forward. However, those following the case closely would likely agree that Apple might pursue a deal particularly attractive to Epic while limiting any concessions to Epic alone.

In fact, Epic's response pre-emptively shuts down this idea, stating that Apple's "serious settlement proposal" must "benefit all developers," and hinting at the end of its response that Apple's efforts may be too late.
